articles.title: Mike Lynch’s superyacht had unidentified vulnerability to high winds, report finds
articles.summary: Bayesian, which sank off Sicily killing seven including tech tycoon, had not been fully assessed, say investigators
body: The superyacht Bayesian, which sank in a storm off Sicily killing seven people including the tech tycoon Mike Lynch and his teenage daughter, was vulnerable to knockdown but crew were not aware as it had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down, the final report from the UK’s Marine Accident Investigations Branch (MAIB) has said.
The 56-metre (184ft) vessel was anchored near the fishing port of Porticello when it sank during a violent storm shortly before dawn on 19 August 2024.

Lynch, 59, had been enjoying a voyage around Sicily with family and friends after his acquittal in a long-running fraud case regarding the sale of the technology company he founded, Autonomy, to Hewlett-Packard in 2011.

He and his 18-year-old daughter, Hannah, died, as did lawyer Chris Morvillo and his wife, Neda, banker Jonathan Bloomer and his wife, Judy, and the yacht’s chef, Recaldo Thomas. Nine other crew members and six guests were rescued.
The MAIB final report, published on Thursday, appears to contrast with recent reports from Italy, where prosecutors have reportedly blamed errors by the crew.

The MAIB report details how the yacht was hit “by extreme winds that were not explicitly forecast” of about 70 knots (80 mph), which knocked it on to its side in less than 15 seconds. It sank 18 minutes later.

Investigators found that the yacht’s vulnerability to strong winds had never been assessed for the conditions in which it was anchored, with its sails down and its retractable centreboard raised. The centreboard is a large underwater structure that helps a sailing vessel remain stable.
The extreme weather was most likely caused by a downburst – a powerful blast of air from a thunderstorm that hits the sea and spreads out with enormous force, the report said.

None of the life rafts on board automatically inflated or released from the vessel. The crew managed to release one manually. Survivors were rescued by crew from a nearby yacht, the Sir Robert Baden-Powell.

Rob Loder, the chief inspector of MAIB, said: “This accident developed with extraordinary speed. In just 14 minutes, calm conditions had given way to winds of at least 68 knots, which in less than 15 seconds pushed the yacht on to its side.

“Our investigation found that Bayesian had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised, because the yacht had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down. The extreme winds that night were also not explicitly forecast, so the crew had no warning of the risk.”

The report conveys the desperate minutes as the Bayesian was knocked down. Crew were alerted by sudden and severe winds of up to 30 knots at 03.55, and within two minutes the yacht listed starboard and the vessel began to drag anchor before the wind suddenly increased to about 70 knots.

“At 04.06 Bayesian violently heeled over 90 degrees to starboard, taking less than 15 seconds to do so. People, furniture and loose items fell across the deck. The generators shut down immediately and battery-supplied emergency lighting automatically turned on,” the report said.

Some guests, awoken by the listing and who had left their cabins, escaped. One couple used furniture drawers as an improvised ladder. Guests who managed to get to the flying bridge were instructed to swim away from the vessel and warned to stay clear of the mast and boom as it sank.

Passengers and crew who made it out gathered in the water, using a torch on a mobile to search for others. A crew member managed to swim back to the yacht to manually release one life raft from stowage. By 04.24 the life raft was inflated.

The investigation found that, with no sails set, Bayesian was vulnerable to knockdown in severe winds. This vulnerability was affected by its loading condition, apparent wind angle and the position of the centreboard, but had not been identified in the originally approved stability information available to the crew.

It said information contained in guidance provided to mariners did not provide sufficient detail of the impact of possible weather conditions to support decision-making. The weather forecast also did not indicate the risk of downbursts from the thunderstorms it predicted, it said.
Inquest proceedings in the UK are looking at the deaths of Mike and Hannah Lynch and Jonathan and Judy Bloomer, who were all British nationals.
The Maritime and Coastguard Agency is also investigating the sinking.

articles.title: Crimea bridge has been attacked again, says Russian-installed governor
articles.summary: Assessment of damage is underway, days after two attacks that destroyed road section of key bridge across Kerch strait linking annexed peninsula to Russia
body: A key bridge connecting annexed Crimea to Russia has been attacked again, a Russian-appointed regional governor has said, two days after Ukrainian strikes caused serious damage to it.

“Following a new attack on the Crimean Bridge, traffic has been temporarily halted. All relevant services are on site and at work. An assessment of the damage is under way,” Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, wrote on Telegram.

Wednesday’s ‌attack is third this week on the highly symbolic bridge that links Russia with Crimea, which ​it seized from Ukraine in 2014. A 227-metre section of the road spanning the Kerch strait was destroyed this week, but the rail corridor appears to be operable despite sustaining some damage.
Related: ‘They were keeping it for a rainy day’: Ukraine’s Kerch bridge attack is proof Kyiv still has cards to play

The strike comes just hours before an unprecedented meeting between Russian president Vladimir Putin and his Chinese and American counterparts, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump, in China. One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said this week’s attacks were designed to embarrass Putin on the world stage. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.

For Ukraine, the bridge is a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Ukraine has previously declared that the bridge across the Kerch strait, built eight years ago, is illegal. Kyiv had tried twice to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.

Earlier, Ukraine critically damaged the road section of the bridge in what President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed as an “unprecedented” military operation. A span of the bridge’s road section collapsed, but the railway line was still standing.

Zelesnkyy described the earlier attack as the culmination of a long and complex campaign to demolish the bridge, involving domestically produced drones and ballistic missiles. Palianytsia drones hit the road section of the bridge, while Neptune and other missiles targeted the adjacent rail section, he added.

articles.title: Israeli tanks cross ‘yellow line’ boundary into Hamas-controlled central Gaza
articles.summary: First incursion across boundary since ceasefire deal comes as Eisenkot seeks to form government without Netanyahu
body: The Israeli military crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza on Wednesday in its first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed last October, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.

Israeli tanks rolled along the Salah al-Din road, Gaza’s main north-south route, a day after the US-backed Board of Peace, a body overseeing the ceasefire, accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities.
An Israeli military spokesperson said troops were carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of the yellow line in central Gaza.

The military ​has not commented extensively on the operation, which came as the Israeli opposition politician, Gadi Eisenkot, has been seeking to form a government without the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his political reputation on promises to keep Israel safe.
Related: Children at risk as ‘weaponisation of aid’ surges in conflict zones, analysis finds

A Gaza security source told AFP there was “intense Israeli artillery shelling” north of Nuseirat refugee camp and reported Israeli military vehicles in central Gaza “amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes since midday”.

Hamas condemned the Israeli raid and the forced displacement of Palestinians as “a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement” and a dangerous escalation. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Hamas’s statement.
Residents reported hearing tank fire in the area. Palestinian medics said one person was killed in an Israeli airstrike near the site of the raid.

In separate incidents on Wednesday, Palestinian medics said two people were killed by Israeli fire, one in Deir al-Balah and the other in Gaza City. The Israeli military said it was unaware of any incident in Deir al-Balah and had struck a militant in Gaza City.
Israel has stepped up its attacks on Hamas, which it says has been regrouping and rearming. Hamas has accused Israel of trying to derail the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025.
Israeli strikes have continued since the ceasefire, and Hamas remains armed.
Last week, an Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a surgeon and a disabled man, and wounded 28 others, according to the hospital director.
Related: Palestinian woman shot dead by Israeli settlers near Jericho, witnesses say

The body overseeing Donald Trump’s plan to end the war in Gaza has accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities, leaving Palestinians in dire conditions and the ceasefire at risk of collapse.

In its second report to the UN security council since the truce began 13 months ago, the Trump-led Board of Peace said the gap between what was agreed and what was happening on the ground remained the biggest threat to the deal. The report, seen by Reuters, warned that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely”.
Gaza’s health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire came into effect. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.

Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its military campaign in response to the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed.
Reuters and AFP contributed to this report

articles.title: EU proposes €45bn loan for Ukraine to avert cash crisis and boost defences
articles.summary: Von der Leyen says she wants to give Kyiv ‘strong hand’ in talks and is confident all 27 member states will back idea
body: The EU executive has proposed a €45bn (£37.5bn) loan for Ukraine to help with a looming cash crisis and reinforce its defences, as Russia’s relentless bombardment continues.

Announcing the plan to lend Kyiv the money in 2027, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said: “We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiating table. And Ukraine only needs to repay once Russia pays for the damage it has caused in Ukraine.”
She expressed confidence all 27 member states would stand behind the loan, despite four central and eastern European countries having already ruled themselves out.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he hoped for the swift adoption of the loan and was counting on the support of all EU member states: “Strong support for Ukraine is the best signal to Russia that this war must end,” he wrote on X.
Zelenskyy convinced EU leaders last month that his country faced a €70bn funding gap in 2027. The EU pledged to cover €45bn and wants Ukraine’s other allies to cover the rest.

Only 11 months ago, the EU agreed a €90bn loan for Ukraine, which was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s military and civilian needs in 2026 and 2027. But as Russia’s attacks have escalated, the cost of Ukraine’s defence and the toll of economic disruption continue to rise.

Andrius Kubilius, the EU defence commissioner, said Ukraine’s military spending was increasingly dominated by drones. Ukraine, he told reporters, expected Russia to use 10m drones this year and 20m in 2027. “Ukraine with EU assistance needs to match – and will match,” he said.
The EU loan is split into two parts: €25bn for weapons and €20bn for civilian needs, including funding essential services, such as schools and hospitals.

Von der Leyen expressed confidence that all member states would support the loan because “all 27 member states say very clearly that they want to support Ukraine”. She said member states could choose to support Ukraine’s civilian needs, rather than military spending.

Slovakia, Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria, however, have said they do not intend to take part in the latest funding round for Ukraine, prompting a warning from the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, that he would block the EU’s seven-year budget unless all countries got onboard.
The four central and eastern countries are net beneficiaries of the EU budget, while Germany is the largest payer and Ukraine’s biggest EU donor.
The EU wants Ukraine’s non-EU allies – such as Norway, the UK and Canada – to find €25bn for Kyiv in 2027.

The EU proposal included provisions “to help other countries to help us”, a senior commission official said. Brussels has proposed that G7 countries that provide new loans get guarantees that the borrowing can be repaid with future profits from Russia’s frozen assets.
The profits from the Russian assets are being used to repay a €45bn loan issued by the G7 to Ukraine in 2024.

Countries with a triple-A credit rating could opt to provide guarantees to the EU budget up to €5bn to expand European borrowing for Ukraine on capital markets. The commission has identified six countries that fall into this category: Australia, Canada, Liechtenstein, Norway, Singapore and Switzerland.

EU officials previously said the UK and other allies needed to do more to support Ukraine in 2027, arguing that the EU was shouldering too much of the burden. The UK subsequently pledged a £10bn economic and military support package for Ukraine.

Zelenskyy said: “The UK, Canada, Japan, and Norway have been helping tremendously in our defence of life, and establishing clear rules under which they can provide further aid in conjunction with the EU will help even more.”

Britain said on Wednesday night it would send 1,000 long-range attack drones to Ukraine as part of a further £260m military aid package, a day before prime minister Andy Burnham was due to travel to Berlin to co-chair a meeting of Kyiv’s European allies.

The commitment to support Ukraine’s deep strike campaign into Russia emerged a day after the US argued that Kyiv’s attacks on refineries and warehouses were ineffective and counter-productive, earning criticism from the UK and Germany.
“The UK will do everything we can to ensure Ukraine is able to defend itself,” Burnham said.

articles.title: FAA chief urges critics to ‘lay off’ Sean Duffy for flight stoppage: ‘Blame me’
articles.summary: Bryan Bedford’s comments come as Duffy, Trump transport secretary, faces scrutiny over handling of outage crisis
body: The head of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) took responsibility for the nationwide ground stop that affected more than 12,400 flights on Friday, urging people to “lay off” Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary.
“I take full responsibility for it,” Bryan Bedford, the FAA administrator, said at an aviation event staged by the Hill on Wednesday.
“I wish people would lay off the secretary,” Bedford added. “He’s got a lot of work to do, but I’m the guy they hired to get this done. So blame me if we need to blame somebody. Blame me.”

The FAA administrator’s comments arrived as Duffy, the top transportation official in the US, faces scrutiny from former officials and lawmakers over his handling of the tech outage crisis, which left tens of thousands of travelers stranded over the weekend.
Related: US senators urge White House AI chief to fix vulnerabilities after mass outages

In a press conference on Friday, Duffy refused to accept responsibility or apologize for the crisis, blaming Democratic lawmakers and his predecessors for not providing the funding to upgrade outdated systems.
The FAA said it grounded all flights after a newly installed router flooded communication systems, causing problems between aircraft systems and radar feeds.
Trump administration officials have emphasized that the tech outage at the FAA was not caused by a cybersecurity attack and was unrelated to other disruptions.

Jay Clayton, director of national intelligence, testified on Wednesday that there was no indication the outage was the result of a malicious actor or connected to similar disruptions that have affected banks and major companies. He said the outages were caused by patches – modifications to systems to address issues such as security vulnerabilities.

But lawmakers, including some Republicans, have grown frustrated with Duffy after he and the White House asked Congress to provide $50bn in funding to upgrade the air traffic system, more than double what was originally estimated.
Some GOP lawmakers told reporters the justification behind the large sum of money was thin.
But Bedford argued the investment was necessary on Wednesday, claiming Donald Trump and Duffy believed the outage was a “call to action” to “fix the system” and “return to the gold standard”.

articles.title: Hegseth uses Venezuela visit to boast of Maduro’s capture by US military
articles.summary: Defense secretary asserts US dominance on trip that would have seemed ‘impossible, almost unbelievable’ a year ago
body: Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.

Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999.

Speaking outside the recently reopened US embassy in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Wednesday, Hegseth said: “It’s a great honor to be here as the first United States secretary of war this century to set foot in Venezuela.​ Just one year ago my presence here … would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable.

“In fact, exactly one year ago today … [Maduro] stood on a stage not too far from here and yelled mockingly, ‘Come and get me!’” Hegseth recalled, before adding sarcastically: “Well, we answered that call.
“The reality is that … January 3 is the day that will go down in history as a day of liberation for Venezuela,” Hegseth claimed, although Maduro’s allies continue to hold power with US support.
Earlier in the day, Hegseth was welcomed to the Miraflores Palace by Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who became acting president with Donald Trump’s blessing after his abduction.

In the aftermath of the deadly US attack, Hegseth was one of the bluntest Trump administration voices when it came to celebrating the invasion. “Maduro had his chance … he effed around and he found out,” the defense secretary bragged.
Speaking at the palace, Hegseth struck a more conciliatory tone as he vowed to deepen cooperation with Venezuela’s new leaders in brief comments that were broadcast by the state broadcaster VTV.

“I stand here on behalf of President Trump, who sends his greeting and looks forward to the opportunities, not just militarily … but also economically: the incredible resource capabilities that your country has, that we look forward to unlocking together with you,” Hegseth told Rodríguez and senior cabinet members, including the defense and foreign ministers, Gustavo González López and Oliver Blanco.

Hegseth said his visit to Rodríguez’s “beautiful country” was designed to re-establish and increase “defense cooperation” between “two great militaries” that less than a year ago were briefly at war. Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that Trump officials were trying to negotiate a long-term US troop presence in Venezuela as part of their push for regional hegemony.

“I appreciate your leadership and commitment to your country,” Hegseth told Maduro’s successor, a once outspoken anti-imperialist leftist who has overseen an unlikely realignment with Washington since her ally was grabbed.

During her five-minute address, Rodríguez, whose oil-rich country is widely seen to have become a US protectorate after January’s invasion, made no mention of Maduro, who is behind bars in New York City.

But referring indirectly to his capture and the subsequent reconciliation with Washington, she told Hegseth: “Thanks to the political and geopolitical maturity of our governments, we have – in a very short period of time, just a few months – turned what were very difficult and very tough times for our people, into an extraordinary space for cooperation and mutual benefit.”

Rodríguez hailed the “historic” energy deal her government recently struck with Trump, who has called it “the biggest oil deal in world history” as well as “the spoils” of his “conquest” of Venezuela.
Hegseth claimed the agreement, which reportedly involves 65bn barrels of reserves, “makes the strait of Hormuz a non-factor for the western hemisphere”.

Critics of Rodríguez’s political movement painted Hegseth’s visit as a humiliating act of genuflection for a president with no choice but to roll out the red carpet for the man whose troops captured her boss.
Writing on X, Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent Venezuelan journalist, said Hegseth’s visit was designed to underscore Washington’s “direct administration” of her country.

“Ten months after Nicolás Maduro’s capture, Washington no longer needs to fire shots to remind everyone who is in charge: the mere presence on Venezuelan soil of the architect of the January incursion reaffirms that the country’s operational sovereignty is subject to the White House’s directives,” Reyes said.

Reyes suspected the visit also carried a message for members of Venezuela’s armed forces. “Domestically, the trip forces the military high command to legitimize the man who directed the extraction of their former commander in chief,” she said. “In this regard, I wonder whether it might be a message of discipline intended to prevent any pockets of resistance in the barracks.”

Trump’s attempts to expand his Shield of the Americas anti-cartel coalition of Latin American governments suffered a major blow last month with the defeat of his far-right ally, Flávio Bolsonaro, in Brazil’s presidential election. The leftwing winner, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has indicated his country will not join the initiative.

But Venezuela’s interim government is in little position to resist. During his surprise visit to Venezuela, Hegseth said Venezuela had gone from being “our most aggressive regional threat to [being] a compliant security partner”. He praised Rodríguez for working “closely, pragmatically, and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela”. Hegseth claimed US and Venezuelan armed forces would work together to attack “narco-terrorists” operating on Venezuelan soil, vowing: “We will hunt you down. We will find you. And we will kill you.”
Concluding her speech at the palace, Rodríguez told her foe-turned-friend: “Thank you, secretary, and I wish you a lifetime of happiness.”

articles.title: Xi Jinping rallies against protectionism as he welcomes Trump to Apec summit
articles.summary: Chinese president greets US counterpart with rare hug before blockbuster trilateral meeting with Putin
body: China’s Xi Jinping rallied Asia-Pacific nations against trade protectionism on Wednesday morning before heading to the airport to welcome Donald Trump, whose administration has just further restricted advanced chip exports, with a rare hug.

The Chinese president spent Wednesday’s opening day of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit switching lanes between multilateralist and big-power politics, culminating in a group photo where he stood central among fellow leaders. He was flanked by Trump and Vladimir Putin – whose blockbuster trilateral meeting will dominate Thursday’s proceedings as the summit gets to its business end.
Having all delegates in the photograph was a tightrope feat in itself, with potential Canadian and Australian refusals to stand with Putin over the war in Ukraine shelved out of respect for the host.

The Russian president did not arrive in a conciliatory mood, using his speech at the summit to call western powers “former hegemons”, state that Europe was in “a humiliating decline” and proclaim that sanctions no longer worked.

However, toasting his varied visitors at a welcoming banquet, Xi invoked “the grand plan for Asia-Pacific cooperation”. Thursday would see those gathered “discuss measures to expand mutual openness, explore pathways for innovation-driven growth, [and] broaden opportunities for pragmatic cooperation in various fields,” he said.
Openness was the main theme of his keynote address, presenting China as a stalwart of free trade and technological innovation.

“We find ourselves in a changing and turbulent world. Global growth lacks momentum, and unilateralism and protectionism are rampant,” he told the audience of business executives and Apec leaders. “We should firmly safeguard the WTO-centred, rules-based multilateral trading system, support free and open trade and investment, and keep global industrial and supply chains stable and unimpeded.”

Critics of Beijing have long accused it of hypocrisy on this point, noting the obstacles many foreign businesses face entering China’s vast market. But Xi’s messaging on open trade was echoed by other leaders who took to the stage after him, including South Korea’s Lee ⁠Jae Myung and Malaysia’s Anwar Ibrahim.
Putin meanwhile took aim at sanctions, claiming they had “largely run their course, having ⁠lost much of their intimidating power”.
That prompted a rebuttal from Canada’s Mark Carney, who told reporters Putin was “lying”. “Sanctions are very real and they’re going to continue to increase as long as this war goes on,” he said.

When Xi met Putin though, he called for closer political and military ties between Russia and China, in a continued demonstration of a tight relationship that has only deepened since Moscow invaded Ukraine in 2022.

Before Putin’s arrival in China, Russia sent nuclear-capable bombers to an airport in Vietnam, in a rare deployment interpreted as a pointed show of Moscow’s ability to project strength in the region despite being embroiled in the Ukraine war. Russian military aircraft had spooked air forces in both Taiwan and Japan on Tuesday as they flew past them while routeing south from Russia’s Far East region.

It was Xi’s reception of Trump, complete with an embrace, that broke with convention; the reception on the airport tarmac is believed to be the first by a Chinese leader in decades, although during Xi’s state visit to Washington in September, Trump had also taken the unusual step of greeting Xi on the tarmac.

Xi travelled to the airport despite the US announcing on Monday new interim rules to further restrict Beijing’s access to advanced semiconductors. That followed an awkward week of news after the chief executive of US chipmaker Nvidia resigned over an affair, reportedly with a woman some US officials suspect of being a Chinese spy.

Beijing’s “overriding objective” was “extending the fragile calm in the US-China relationship for as long as possible”, Ryan Hass, from the Brookings thinktank, told the AFP news agency. “[The reception] set a positive tone for Trump’s visit, marking a contrast from the swirl of news around the Jensen Huang scandal that preceded Trump’s arrival in Shenzhen.”
The state news agency Xinhua said Xi had noted “China is a nation with a tradition of courtesy that values reciprocating goodwill”, after Trump met Xi at the airport when he visited the US.

Trump and Xi will hold a bilateral meeting as well as talks with Putin on Thursday. On Wednesday, the Associated Press reported that Trump had said he and Putin would meet separately as well, citing an anonymous US official.
These meetings will dominate the day’s schedule and the news cycle, a fact that has at times seemed to bother China.

“The Chinese actually tried to have this meeting not happen … They kind of got jammed into it. Then, when it was going to happen, they just wanted statements,” the former US national security adviser Jake Sullivan said on The Rest is Politics podcast. “They are going to be deeply uncomfortable throughout this because this does not fit their narrative of a country that believes in multi-alignment, the United Nations, everyone around the table.”

Shen Weizhong, a former policy planner with China’s foreign ministry who now works for the Global Governance Institution, a Beijing-based thinktank, told the Guardian he would not be surprised if Sullivan was right and that China was “torn”.
Related: Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up?

“On the one hand, it will steal the spotlight. The outcome is not clear and there are no immediate deliverables,” he said. “But on the other side, it will help China’s image – it is the only facilitator who could do this, and if it can ease tensions on the world stage, that will be good.” He said he suspected enthusiasm from both Putin and Trump for the meeting could have ultimately swayed Beijing.

China is actively opposing the framing of the meetings as a new Yalta, the 1945 meeting between Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt that in effect carved up postwar Europe. “The global south will not like having a Yalta 2.0, and China is always taking the smaller countries into consideration,” said Shen.

Also potentially on Thursday’s agenda is an Apec joint statement that, an official told Reuters, delegates were “working around the clock” to find agreement on. “China as host will want something,” said Shen, though even Beijing is “not as obsessed with such deliverables” these days.

articles.title: The Quechua rapper and an artistic movement reclaiming language of the Incas
articles.summary: Renata Flores has gained global recognition for her music in Indigenous language whose speakers have faced social stigma
body: With her long black hair braided into beaded plaits, a delicate silver nose ring, and intricately patterned Andean textile draped around her chest above baggy, low-riding jeans, Renata Flores is a visual reflection of her music: a fusion of traditional and transgressive, old and new, rural and urban.

Nicknamed the “queen of Quechua rap”, Flores, 25, has earned global recognition for mixing Peru’s main Indigenous language and Andean instruments with the urban beats of trap, rap, hip-hop and reggaeton.

She rose to fame as a teenager singing covers in Quechua, the language used by the Incas and South America’s most widespread Indigenous language, with 8 million speakers along the spine of the Andes, half of them in Peru.

Her version of Michael Jackson’s The Way You Make Me Feel, which she translated into Quechua with the help of her grandmothers, became a viral hit on YouTube, launching her into the limelight at the age of 14.

Since that early start, she has molded her musical identity around Quechua, a language she chose to learn from her grandmothers, as her parents did not teach her due to social stigma and the fear that she could face discrimination.

“I feel happy and free when I sing in Quechua, with a strong sense of identity and empowerment,” she said. “Before, I’d say to myself: maybe I should sing in Spanish or English so that more people would listen to me. But I decided to carry on singing in Quechua.”
Her music now tackles darker, more complex themes: marginalisation, women’s rights and state oppression. It focuses on her identity as a Quechua woman and pays homage to the legacy of her forebears.
“I grew up hearing my grandmothers and my mother sing [in Quechua] but rap gave me the chance to say a lot of powerful, difficult things; to protest, too; and to tell the truth.”
Flores is finishing her second album, Kachnanikuraqmi, which means “we are still here” in Quechua. It is a message of hope, resilience and identity for the younger generation, she said.

Following Flores’s example, a vibrant and youthful Quechua-speaking artistic movement has taken hold in Ayacucho, nestled in the southern Andes, with many emerging artists choosing to reclaim the marginalised language.

“Renata is a major pioneer who represented – and continues to represent – our Quechua culture,” said Kayfex, an Ayacucho-born DJ and music producer, who won a Latin Grammy in 2023 and was later signed by Warner Music in the US.

“Music is very global these days and I think expectations are changing too,” he added as he mixed a booming bass track with the plaintive Andean harp and the chiming metallic clink of the iron rods used by traditional Quechua scissor dancers on one of Flores’s songs.

Ayacucho was at the centre of Peru’s bloody conflict between the fanatical Shining Path insurgents and brutal state security forces in the 1980s and 90s, during which nearly 70,000 people died. Tens of thousands more lost loved ones or were forcibly displaced, like Flores’s grandparents.

Patricia Rivera, Flores’s mother and her manager, said: “If you spoke Quechua, people assumed you were from a rural area, and if you were from a rural area you were a terrorist – it was like that. So the fact that people now sing and speak Quechua is a way of reclaiming the language. To say ‘we are Quechua’ with pride – we’re not terrorists.”

Flores is too young to remember that period, but political violence in Peru is by no means over. In December 2022, 10 people were killed and more than 60 injured when soldiers opened fire on protesters in Ayacucho during demonstrations against the government of the then president, Dina Boluarte.

“It was heartbreaking for many families,” said Flores, whose new album includes a song dedicated to the families of the victims. “Let’s say that I’m a transgressor and traditional – I like it when people tell me that I can be both,” she added.

articles.title: Who speaks for Europe abroad? Not its top diplomat
articles.summary: EU leaders’ decision to exclude the bloc’s foreign policy chief from their negotiating lineup for Russia peace talks reveals how national turf wars undermine Brussels’ global ambitions
body: The EU, we are repeatedly told, wants (and needs) to be a global player, a geopolitical heavyweight capable of shaping its own foreign and security policies – or at the very least, speaking with one clear, unambiguous voice on the world stage.

Last Friday’s summit in Dublin, when leaders debated who should represent the bloc in talks aimed at ending Russia’s war on Ukraine – the gravest security crisis the EU has faced in decades – showed once again that it is unlikely to find such a voice anytime soon.

The EU has a chief diplomat: she is called Kaja Kallas, she is a former Estonian prime minister, and she was appointed the EU’s High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, and a European Commission vice-president, in 2024.

In theory, Kallas should embody this more assertive Europe. But as the US-mediated talks accelerate, EU leaders have – despite Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s pleas for the bloc to field a single negotiator – locked her out of the room.

Instead, alongside US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Europe is being represented by a seven-strong team: European Council president António Costa, Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, and representatives from the E5 powers: France, Germany, Britain, Poland, and Italy, working with Nato.

On paper, Kallas’s job description is straightforward and twofold. She chairs the Foreign Affairs Council, the monthly decision-making forum where national foreign ministers meet to agree on common EU foreign policy, sanctions and crisis responses.

She also runs the European External Action Service (EEAS), the bloc’s permanent diplomatic corps and de facto foreign ministry, made up of civil servants and over 140 embassies around the world that carry out day-to-day EU diplomacy on the ground.

In practice, being the face of EU foreign policy – a role created by the Lisbon Treaty in 2009 to answer Henry Kissinger’s famous if apocryphal question “Who do I call when I want to talk to Europe?” – is, as one commentator puts it, a “poisoned chalice”.

Jennifer Rankin in Brussels tells me: “Personally, I think Kallas has an impossible job: having to represent the positions of 27 member states that often disagree on foreign policy, and don’t want to cede real decision making on it to the EU.”

Relations between Kallas and von der Leyen – who critics accuse of sharing exactly the same kind of power-hoarding and centralising instincts as some EU national leaders – have been particularly difficult.

That friction has been aggravated by active proposals in Brussels to overhaul the bloc’s whole diplomatic service, folding parts of the EEAS and key foreign policy powers directly into the Commission president’s remit.

On Friday, when the Dublin summit convened, Kallas was unequivocal: leaders had agreed in 2024, when it was clear there would have to be talks with Russia, “that I’mthe one who is representing Europe in foreign and security policy,” she said.
But when Costa announced the bloc’s negotiators in Dublin, Kallas wasn’t among them. So why did the 27 capitals bypass the person they hired for the job?
Three explanations are doing the diplomatic rounds. First, several western European capitals view the Estonian envoy as too overtly, and fiercely, anti-Russian.

Second, there is a much deeper reflex at play: the EU’s big member states simply refuse to cede real foreign policy power to Brussels. Paris and Berlin in particular resist a single EU envoy, clearly preferring to protect their own seats at the table.
Third, diplomats point to a wider trend for the kind of international questions once handled by foreign ministers being taken over by premiers or presidents.

Whatever the reason, von der Leyen’s defence of the decision was brisk: “We decide for ourselves who will represent us, and we made that decision today,” she said. Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has also argued that intergovernmental formats like the E3 – France, Germany and the UK – are “a well-established format” and “I see absolutely no problem with keeping it that way.”

Others, though, were less happy. Spain and Lithuania both criticised the team approach. “Europe needs one voice,” said Lithuania’s foreign minister, Kęstutis Budrys. “We cannot speak with 27 microphones. We need one.”

All this may seem rather inside-the-Brussels-beltway stuff. But beneath it lies a real, and important debate over whether the EU will ever be a global actor, or be fated to remain a disjointed collection of national voices.

Defenders of the Dublin decision argue that hard security and ending the war are issues that belong to the EU’s major military and financial powers, not supranational officials: bringing the big beasts to the table provides the real geopolitical heft.

One EU diplomat said the problem was that EU institutions “do not have sufficient political legitimacy in the eyes of voters. And this matters big time. The E5 solution is an attempt to bridge that gap.”
But critics see a damaging own goal, and a profound hypocrisy. Brussels commenter Dave Keating argues there is a fatal contradiction inherent in Europe’s integration.

Member states “know what the right thing to do is in the abstract, so they create these positions and institutions to make a stronger EU,” he says. “But then … they undermine [them] … because they always give in to the urge not to hand over power to someone else.”

By choosing to field what Keating called a “European cacophony” that would inevitably be dismissed as irrelevant by Moscow and Washington, leaders proved Kallas’s job “is not real, and the EU doesn’t actually have a foreign policy”, he said.

Jennifer is slightly less damning. “I think the E5+ format could be seen as a realistic answer to represent the EU as it is, not the idealised union of the treaties,” she said. “It needn’t be a cacophony if everyone in the room has the same message.”
So far, on Ukraine at least, there is a large degree of consensus. But if, for example, Marine Le Pen becomes French president, all bets are off,” says Jennifer.

For her part, Kallas has put a brave face on it, insisting she will focus on “substance” while leaders handle “format”. But the suspicion remains: Europe’s leaders want the bloc to be a global power, but won’t let anyone else speak for them.
Until they do, the risk is that the EU will be stuck on the diplomatic sidelines, forever punching below its geopolitical weight.

articles.title: Spanish court investigates Julio Iglesias over sexual abuse claims
articles.summary: Case involving allegations from two women employed at singer’s properties in Caribbean had been shelved
body: A Spanish court is investigating the singer Julio Iglesias over complaints that he sexually abused and physically assaulted two female employees who worked at his properties in the Caribbean.

The announcement of the investigation by the Audiencia Nacional comes almost 11 months after Spanish prosecutors shelved the women’s complaints, arguing the country’s courts had no jurisdiction as the alleged offences took place outside Spain.

But the human rights NGO Women’s Link Worldwide, which is representing the women, has successfully argued that the Audiencia Nacional has jurisdiction over the case and Iglesias’s Spanish nationality provides sufficient grounds to try the case in Spain. It filed a new criminal complaint on the women’s behalf on 3 September.

The allegations emerged in January this year after a three-year joint investigation by the Spanish news site elDiario.es and the Spanish-language TV network Univision Noticias, which gathered testimony from 15 former employees who worked for the now 83-year-old singer between the late 1990s and 2023.

The two complainants – a domestic worker and a physical therapist who were employed at Iglesias’s mansions in the Dominican Republic and the Bahamas – allege the veteran entertainer subjected them “to inappropriate touching, insults and humiliation … in an atmosphere of control and constant harassment”. The offences are alleged to have occurred in 2021.

In a statement released on Wednesday, the Audiencia Nacional said it was investigating the women’s complaint, which accuses Iglesias of “offences against sexual freedom, as well as offences involving bodily harm and degrading treatment”.
The investigating judge, Antonio Piña, said preliminary evidence offered by one of the complainants was sufficient to launch an investigation.

“A photograph of the complainant shows a bruise on one of her arms, consistent with her having been gripped forcefully,” said Piña. “In the same photograph, two marks are visible on one of her thighs – marks that could correspond to a human bite – which the complaint states are the result of her being forced to participate in sexual acts.”

The judge said the “detailed” account submitted, taken with the preliminary evidence provided, was “sufficient to initiate proceedings, without this implying any evaluative judgment regarding the complaint’s credibility”.

However, Piña rejected the women’s allegations of human trafficking and labour offences, and also noted that some of the alleged offences may have expired under the statute of limitations. The judge has called the two women to give evidence in person on 3 February next year.
Iglesias, who has sold more than 300m records during his six-decade career, has denied all the allegations and said he would defend himself against what he described as “a serious affront”.

In a statement posted on Instagram in January, Iglesias wrote: “With great regret, I am responding to the allegations from two people who used to work in my house. I have never abused, coerced or disrespected any woman. These accusations are absolutely false and pain me deeply.”
Women’s Link said the case showed the need for states to ensure access to justice.

“Everyone has the right to have justice systems investigate facts when there are indications of alleged human rights violations,” said Jovana Ríos Cisneros, the NGO’s executive director. “The Spanish state has an obligation to guarantee equal access to justice, regardless of who the accused person is.”

• Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

articles.title: Israel delays building contracts for West Bank settlement after UK sanctions
articles.summary: Attorney general says E1 settlement decision should not be taken by caretaker government led by Netanyahu
body: Israel has postponed issuing contracts for the construction of a large settlement on the West Bank seen as likely to render a two-state solution unviable, days after the UK imposed sanctions against building firms operating in the area.

Israeli diplomats insisted the move was not in response to the measures from Downing Street. Gali Baharav-Miara, the attorney general, said any decision on settlement expansion should not be taken by the caretaker government led by Benjamin Netanyahu but by whatever new administration was formed.

She ordered the Israel land authority and ministry of housing not to open the tender process. Israeli diplomats suggested the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, had acted prematurely on Monday in sanctioning the eight construction firms. But UK diplomats believe the growing political pressure on Israel over settlements, including from US Democrats, is having an impact.

The deferral puts the E1 settlement expansion in the mix for any coalition negotiations. The leader of the Change bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, seen as Israel’s most likely next prime minister, has been clear in opposing violent settler activity, as has the newly elected Knesset speaker, Matan Kahana, an ally of Eisenkot.

Eisenkot has also opposed the E1 settlement expansion, describing it as a mistake likely to alienate international opinion. He said of the plan: “I recall that Netanyahu himself opposed this for a long time, and due to coalition pressure, he gave in and approved it.”

The EI settlement expansion, due to have been announced on Thursday, has long been seen as qualitatively different since the land – between Jerusalem and Ma’aleh Adumim, a West Bank settlement city of nearly 40,000 residents – bisects the West Bank and cuts it off from East Jerusalem.

Miliband has said it would mark the death knell of a future Palestinian state. The UK, along with a group of European countries, has recently recognised Palestine, and the preservation of a two-state solution has been described as the north star of Labour policy towards the region.

The construction tender was published for more than 3,401 housing units in the area. At the beginning of November, the Israel Defense Forces began demolishing homes in a Bedouin community within the E1 area.
Israel has already enforced the downgrading of the UK consulate in East Jerusalem as a reprisal for Miliband’s decision in September to try to end trade links with the illegal settlements.
Related: Palestinian woman shot dead by Israeli settlers near Jericho, witnesses say

Bennett said: “The British Labour government’s hostility, bias and one-sided approach are particularly glaring given its failure to take any action against the Palestinian Authority, which continues to encourage terrorism through financial payments, promote incitement in its education system and engage in illegal construction in violation of signed agreements.”

Although the Israeli election was largely fought on domestic security-related issues, Eisenkot seems to be more sensitive to the implications of Israel’s crumbling global reputation, and the need to make efforts to be seen to be listening to the criticism.
If he becomes prime minister, Eisenkot will, indirectly at least, also have to take account of the views of the Arab parties even if these parties are not going to become members of the government.

The group Peace Now welcomed the attorney general’s decision: “A government that lost the elections is not permitted to exploit its final days in power to advance destructive moves that will endanger Israel’s future and its international standing.

Construction in E1 is liable to eliminate the possibility of a two-state solution and drag Israel into a severe diplomatic crisis and international sanctions. The AG’s decision is an important step, but the struggle is not over yet.”

articles.title: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
articles.summary: A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza
body: Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.
Related: ‘They showed no mercy’: mapping the Rohingya villages being erased by rebel forces

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.

It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.
The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.

The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.

The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.

The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.

The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.
Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.

Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians.”
In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”

In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”
He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.

Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.

In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically”.
It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.
The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of The Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.
The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.
Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.

On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

articles.title: Russian attacks have left Kyiv with devastating power outages – and its mayor in a perilous position
articles.summary: As Ukraine’s capital suffers through an energy crisis, many blame Vitali Klitschko for failing to prepare for winter
body: Maksym Bakhmatov, the outspoken head of one of Kyiv’s largest city districts, did not mince his words when it came to who was responsible for the devastating power outages plaguing his area’s 600,000 residents.

“First, because of Putin,” he said from his office in Desnianskyi, a working-class area on Kyiv’s left bank. “Second, because of lack of normal management from the mayor, [Vitali Klitschko]. That’s it.”

It may seem unfair to blame a wartime mayor facing daily strikes from Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones for the devastating energy crisis now hitting major Ukrainian cities. Among the worst hit is Kyiv where many homes only have power for four hours a day now, well before the winter months when freezing temperatures will put far more strain on the remaining infrastructure.

This week Russia struck two crucial bridges in Kyiv crossing the Dnipro river with ballistic missiles, threatening to cut off the two sections of the city – part of a broader strategy aiming to sever the western and eastern sections of the country.

But critics argue that the city’s management failed to prepare for the dire power shortages despite clear signs the Kremlin would target Kyiv with strikes that would seek to end its viability as a livable city.

Bakhmatov said some homes had already had power outages of up to 37 hours straight. As a district head, he said he did not have the budget or financing to take on the larger projects that he believed should have been implemented over the past five years – decentralising power generation and finding workarounds to help the city survive another winter of Russian attacks.
“We have no alternative generators in order to generate electricity inside of Kyiv,” he said. “They didn’t build anything for this, and for now we have almost a collapse of city.”
A rare wartime political rally in Kyiv last month gathered about 500 people on the downtown Khreshchatyk street to accuse Klitschko of a number of alleged shortcomings, including the energy crisis.
“Kyiv is in blackout – Klitschko will get knocked out,” read one sign at the rally, referring to the mayor’s history as a boxing champion.
More concerning than that rally may be the mounting political pressure from Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has blamed Klitschko for failing to prepare for the winter season.

“The situation is worst in Kyiv – people and businesses are facing prolonged power and water outages, and the challenges are extremely serious,” Zelenskyy wrote last week in a direct attack on Klitschko’s leadership. “In fact, these are the consequences of the failure to implement decisions at the city level on preparations for the heating season, as well as of this Russian operation against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.”
Klitschko defended himself the same day, asking “How is [Kyiv]… supposed to stop the Russian special operation against the Ukrainian energy system?”

The Guardian has previously reported on intercepted Russian plans to make Kyiv uninhabitable, prescribing strikes with specific drones on power plants and substations that could cut off electricity, heating, water, and even sewage systems, causing the “deterioration of sanitary conditions and the forced outflow of residents from cities.”

Ukraine’s central government is responsible for the defence of most large power plants and other energy infrastructure and the country’s centralised grid means that it is also responsible for trying to keep the lights on and water running in cities around the country.

“The mantra of the central government that Kyiv is the worst, its constant manipulations and lies are a bad story,” Klitschko wrote. “Because in its attempts to get rid of Klitschko by any means necessary … the central government is in fact destroying Kyiv.”

Volodymyr Fesenko, a veteran political analyst, said the “conflict between Zelenskyy and Klitschko is very old and very personal”. It goes back to when Zelenskyy was a standup comic skewering Ukrainian elites, including Klitschko, and continued after he became president in 2019. The two are not known to have met in person since Zelenskyy became president.

“The city really is not ready as compared with other cities, say, Kharkiv,” Fesenko said, noting the lack of follow-through on promises by the Kyiv government including the construction of more bomb shelters. But the central government also answers for the defence of large infrastructure, including bridges, he added. And then there was Putin, he added, who it appeared had “made a conscious decision to try to break us”.

It would be difficult to remove Klitschko as mayor but Zelenskyy’s office had in the past mulled removing Klitschko’s authority over much of the city’s infrastructure, he said. It was not clear if those plans were moving forward at present, and whether Zelenskyy would want to risk further political chaos in an already tense situation.

“There is a risk to Klitschko right now. We will see if Zelenskyy ultimately moves forward with efforts to remove him, but it is probably not Ukraine’s biggest political issue right now,” Fesenko said.

Demonstrators at the rally last month noted that they didn’t want their protest to be construed as helping Russia undermine the political stability in Ukraine. But the anger at Klitschko was on full display. “We’ve learned in Ukraine that changes usually only come when the fire starts,” said one protester with dyed red hair and a long blue coat, who gave her name as Maryana. When asked what she meant by fire, she answered: “Molotov [cocktails].”

Kharkiv, which is about five hours east of Kyiv by car, sits just 19 miles (30km) from the Russian border. In an interview in Kharkiv, the mayor, Ihor Terekhov, said the city faced an even more dire threat than Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities from Russian missiles and cited a “catastrophic” shortage of funding for the efforts to heat the city.
“We have set out on a path to decentralise the system that provides utility services, as well as energy services,” he said.

That would involve taking Kharkiv off the grid by creating “energy islands” – small, fuel-powered generators that can provide electricity for essential services, as well as modular boilers and other workarounds, he said. “It is very costly and time-consuming.”

In Kyiv, Bakhmatov’s office was dark as he spoke. It was adorned with a wall-sized map of his district and plenty of anti-Klitschko posters. He was openly partisan against the current mayor and even said he himself may be a reasonable replacement.

But he said he was most interested in representing the people of his district. Its population of 600,000, he said, would make it one of the largest cities in Ukraine on its own, and there was no workable evacuation plan for local residents. They would need to find a way to live out a cold, dark winter there.
“We need help with the generators, with food, with power stations, and so on,” he said. “Just help us.”

articles.title: The voice of a nation: the Czech children’s TV show that became a symbol of media freedom
articles.summary: Večerníček has wished children goodnight for 60 years, and now his distinctive newspaper hat symbolises the fight for the future of public broadcasting
body: Photos of the mass rallies in support of Czech public broadcasters in recent weeks have featured one detail that has baffled outsiders: demonstrators wearing little hats made out of folded newspapers.
But to Czechs they are instantly recognisable. The hat belongs to Večerníček, a little cartoon boy who appears on Czech Television every evening at 6.45pm.
If you are a Czech child, have had a Czech child or have spent time in the vicinity of one between 6.45pm and 6.55pm, you will know Večerníček.

He doffs his hat, wishes the nation’s children dobrý večer (good evening), and mounts a little flight of stairs in the sky, tossing newspapers from under his arm – Večerníček is the diminutive of večerník, the word for the once-familiar evening newspaper.
He rides a rocking horse, drives a little car and finally pedals a unicycle to a rather trippy soundtrack of vibraphone, electric organ and flute (the programme started in 1965).

There follows a short, animated bedtime story. Stalwarts are Rumcajs the highwayman, Maxipes Fík the enormous dog and, of course, Krtek the Little Mole, fluffy versions of which now stare accusingly at you from the souvenir section of Prague airport.

It’s a nightly ritual for Czech families that marks the transition from playtime to bedtime. Parents across the land wait anxiously for the same jingle to appear, culminating in his final signoff of dobrou noc (goodnight).
That unmistakable voice belongs to Michal Citavý, 68, now a digital nomad who runs a travel business with his wife, Zuzana, and splits his time between south-east Asia, Europe and South Africa.
Related: Hundreds of thousands of Czechs protest in Prague over media freedom

It’s safe to say he has not been glued to coverage of the demonstrations in his native Prague, where hundreds of thousands of people have been turning out since late October to voice opposition to the government’s plans to abolish the licence fees for public TV and radio and fund them instead from the state budget, a move critics fear will diminish media independence.

“My daughters told me what was going on, so I knew about it. But I haven’t really followed it,” said Citavý, speaking from his home near a game reserve about 50km north-east of Pretoria in South Africa. One of his daughters was at Sunday’s demonstration, which proved to be the biggest since the fall of communism in what was then Czechoslovakia in 1989.

Citavý does, however, remember recording those two phrases – dobrý večer and dobrou noc – when he was six, in 1964. “It happened actually in August, basically during the school holidays. I was staying with my grandparents at their weekend house, not far from Prague. And the guys from the film company needed a child to say ‘Dobrý večer, dobrou noc’. I think I was probably the only one who was around during the holidays and relatively close to the city,” said Citavý, who did some TV acting as a child.

“So they sent a car for me and collected me, took me to the TV place where I was repeating those bloody four words and then they brought me back. And that was it. At the time, and for quite some time afterwards, I never even thought about it.”

Since then, Večerníček has survived the upheavals of the Soviet-led invasion, the Velvet Revolution and the dissolution of Czechoslovakia. Its appropriation by those who oppose the government’s plans for Czech Television (and Czech Radio) is particularly resonant: it represents a shared cultural experience rather than an explicitly political cause.

So surely Michal can’t resist telling people he is the voice of Večerníček? “I try not to tell them too much. I hated it when I was, you know, a teenager. Now I don’t really care. My wife likes telling people though,” Michal said.
“She always says that she has a husband that every single one of them knows and could recognise. And that confuses everybody,” said Michal, who has three adult daughters.
“Though when I was away on business it was always nice knowing I could still say goodnight to them every evening.”

articles.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
articles.summary: Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans
body: The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.

Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.

The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.

Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.

In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.

If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).

According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.

In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.

“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”
Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.
The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.

The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.
One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.
In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.

The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.

In order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers shows that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.

On this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU announced the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.
The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.
During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.

Timothy Kaldas, the deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, said the commission had generally “done a poor job of leveraging the funds of European taxpayers to support genuine stabilisation” on the other side of the Mediterranean. “The strategic interest of Europe is seeing a more economically stable Egypt with a population that is less precarious,” he said.

Sandra Gómez López, a Spanish socialist MEP who recently visited Cairo to assess human rights in Egypt, said the data presented by the Guardian raised important questions. “The commission must explain transparently why it considers these commitments to have been fulfilled and demonstrate that European funding is genuinely contributing to improving social protection for the Egyptian population,” she said.
She stressed that the EU should not withdraw support, “but neither can we allow the country’s strategic importance to lead us to lower our standards when it comes to human rights”.

For critics, the questions about the EU’s willingness to hold Egypt accountable on very precise socioeconomic targets do not bode well for the broader but less defined goals for democracy and human rights.

Strik said: “The fact that Egypt and the commission even seem to ignore the crystal-clear socioeconomic conditions doesn’t increase my expectation that they adhere to the vague precondition on democracy and the rule of law.”
Claudio Francavilla, an associate EU director at Human Rights Watch, said: “Without benchmarks, the EU has turned a human rights conditionality into a blank cheque for Egypt’s authoritarianism.”

In a statement to the Guardian, the European Commission said the policy target on Takaful and Karama referred to new beneficiary families “and not to its net increase”. The spokesperson said there was “no contradiction” between this statement and that in a confidential document that said Egypt was required to “further expand cash transfer programmes”.

Asked about the release of the remaining €1.5bn in promised loans, the commission said it “will be made once all conditions have been met”, referring to 24 economic policy conditions, keeping an IMF programme on track and “taking concrete and credible steps towards respecting effective democratic mechanisms, including a multiparty parliamentary system, and the rule of law, and guaranteeing respect for human rights”.
It added: “Compliance with the conditionality is examined thoroughly” by EU officials and diplomats based on “information provided by the Egyptian authorities and other relevant sources”.
Egypt’s mission to the EU in Brussels did not respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: South Korea’s high-stakes university exams upended by AI cheating scandal
articles.summary: South Korea has been gripped by revelations of AI-aided cheating, just days before more than half a million students are to sit high-stakes entrance exams
body: The integrity of South Korea’s career-defining university entrance exam has been thrown into doubt after the top scorer in a recent professional exam admitted using a concealed camera and AI to cheat.

On Thursday, more than half a million people, mostly school students, are due to sit the exam, known as the suneung, at 1,312 centres across the country. The exam runs for a gruelling eight hours over a single day and determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.

The country goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended.

The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre. Extra trains run from 6am, police drive latecomers to their exam halls, and tourist attractions open late to ease traffic. Offices are asked to open at 10am.
Related: 160 questions, only one wrong: top scorer in South Korea tax exam admits AI cheating

But in recent days, exam organisers have faced a renewed threat to the validity of the entire exercise, after the top scorer in this year’s tax accountancy exam- who got just one question wrong out of 160– admitted on Sunday he had cheated by using AI.
Prime minister Han Seong-sook told a cabinet meeting in Seoul on Tuesday that AI-assisted cheating was a “social evil” that the government would “root out”.
“We will block outright the carrying of smart devices during the exam,” she said. The education ministry and other agencies should approach it “as if staking their jobs on it”, she added.

Han said smart devices must be turned off and handed in, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.
The government will also send emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sound at full volume and cannot be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.

More invigilators will be deployed, and the government said it was preparing to switch off school wifi inside exam centres and public wifi nearby, and that personal hotspots, which cannot be blocked, would be traced through connection records.
The weekend’s cheating revelation captured national headlines in South Korea, stoking concern about the security of the suneung.

In a video posted to his lawyer’s YouTube channel, the exam cheat said he had photographed the questions with a concealed microcamera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. “I cheated in the tax accountant exam,” he said. “My top placing is not the result of legitimate effort.”
His lawyer handed police a camera, a laptop and a phone. No charges have been brought, and the prime minister has ordered procedures to begin that would void his result and bar him for five years.

The education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, told parliament on Monday that while authorities could screen out the smart glasses already on sale at Thursday’s exam, newer variants could not be dealt with perfectly.

Choi has ruled out postponing the exam, which has been delayed several times before, including in 2017, after an earthquake struck the south-eastern city of Pohang, and in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic.

Smart glasses have been banned in exams since the end of June. In October, several candidates were caught with them while sitting university-run admissions exams. At the suneung, wearing a pair counts as using one even when switched off.

The education ministry looked at using radio-frequency equipment to detect the glasses in exam halls, but concluded conditions varied too much between venues for deployment this year. Checks will instead rely on visual inspection, with at least one dedicated official placed in each exam centre.

Teachers’ unions have criticised the government response as belated. A survey last month of 2,716 secondary school teachers by the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union showed that 82.3% said they could not tell whether a candidate was wearing smart glasses under the current procedure, with only 3.5% saying they could.

To avoid facing scrutiny on exam day, some candidates are reportedly switching to contact lenses. An optician in Suwon, south of Seoul, said students who had never worn contacts were coming in to ask how to put them in.
Han said on X on Monday that the checks would be handled carefully “so that candidates acting in good faith do not suffer unnecessary anxiety or inconvenience”.
