In his video confession, the accountancy test cheat addressed suneung candidates directly. “The suneung is coming up soon,” he said.
“To anyone thinking of cheating as I did: I am going to tell the investigators everything, so please don’t think, ‘I won’t get caught.’”

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: US criticism of Kyiv’s deep strikes in Russia is ‘quite stupid’, says Germany
articles.summary: Pentagon policy ⁠chief’s comments on Ukraine’s war tactic sparks disagreement at Nato meeting. What we know on day 1,729
body: The Pentagon has warned Ukraine’s western backers that strikes deep inside Russia are counterproductive and urged them to focus their military support on equipment for frontline combat. Germany immediately dismissed the warning as “stupid,” while Britain said the strikes are saving lives. The disagreement came as Ukraine’s supporters met at Nato headquarters on Tuesday to rally support for more arms and ammunition.

Speaking in Brussels, Pentagon policy ⁠chief Elbridge Colby said that “while the public conversation focuses on the spectacle of deep strikes designed to incur pain on the Russian population, our assessment is that ​such strikes have not been effective in driving an end to the war, nor do they contribute to blunting Russia’s advances on the front line.” He warned that deep strikes, “especially those that target ​civilian infrastructure such as Wildberries (the Russian equivalent of Amazon), have ‌actually probably hardened the Russian public’s ​resolve and the Kremlin’s ​own willingness to escalate”. He said his comments did not mean “Ukraine should be forced to fight with its hands tied behind its back”.

Colby added that Ukraine’s army is “very effective” when it focuses on frontline fighting, using drones to slow Russian advances and hit their supply lines. Colby said the US believes “that focusing our support on the frontlines and on associated midrange strikes is the most effective way to enable Ukraine’s defence and thus to set the conditions for an end to the war”.

Asked whether he shared Colby’s position, German defence minister Boris Pistorius said “criticising strikes ⁠like that in Russia to destroy strategic military and military-used targets” was “quite a stupid thing”. “Instead of criticising that, we should rather criticise and talk about ​the terroristic strikes every night and every day on … energy, ‌water, and heating infrastructure in Ukraine,” Pistorius said. British defence minister Wes Streeting took the same line, saying those strikes “helped to degrade Putin’s war ‌machine, buying time and saving lives”. The clash laid bare a widening rift between Washington and its European allies over how Ukraine should ⁠wage the war.

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said ⁠the strike on the ⁠Russian-built ⁠Kerch Bridge linking Crimea ​to Russia was revenge for numerous Russian attacks on Ukrainian bridges, infrastructure ​and cities. “We have ‌long ‌been telling Russia: Enough ‌of striking bridges, cities and villages, energy infrastructure, railways and grain ships. Enough of war. But every ‌time Russia chooses further escalation,” Zelenskyy said in ​his nightly video address. Dan Sabbagh writes that hitting and demolishing the bridge showed that Kyiv still has cards to play in the war.

A European defence company says its missiles were the only ⁠foreign-made weapons used in Ukraine’s attack on the Kerch Bridge, a rare operational role for a western manufacturer ⁠in one of Kyiv’s most ⁠significant long-range ​strikes. Oleksandr Danyliuk, president of Dutch-headquartered startup Destinus, told Reuters ⁠seven of its Ruta cruise missiles hit the bridge during a multistage operation ​that Zelenskyy said took ‌weeks to prepare.

Moldovan president Maia Sandu said on Tuesday ⁠a Russian drone flew over the capital Chisinau, and pledged to press for further sanctions against Moscow. Moldova’s pro-European government has long denounced Russia’s war ⁠in Ukraine and complained ⁠about violations ​of its airspace by drones it has identified as Russian, especially near its border with Ukraine. But drones have rarely come close to the ⁠capital. Sandu wants Moldova to join the EU by 2030.

Finland’s president Alexander Stubb urged European leaders to speak directly with Vladimir Putin, in an interview with the Financial Times. Outsourcing talks with Russia to the US was not a responsible course of action, he told the paper.
A senior American soldier assigned to Nato who was arrested in Britain last week on suspicion of spying for Russia has been transferred to US military custody, writes Nadeem Badshah.

The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) said it had been targeted in a cyber-attack, days after it confirmed Russia would not take part in the under-20 world championships. The IIHF’s official website was still offline late Tuesday, hours after an image of Russian players celebrating had appeared alongside a caption which read: “Scared to face Russia? You banned the only team you can’t beat.” The image was removed from the site, which was later declared “temporarily unavailable” due to “maintenance.”

articles.title: A potato war has been simmering for decades between the US and Japan. It’s about to reach boiling point
articles.summary: Under pressure from Donald Trump, Japan’s government could be about to lift a ban on imported American potatoes, which farmers say would threaten their livelihoods
body: It could be a piping hot croquette eaten on the go, a bowl of nikujaga stew or a plate of home-cooked chips. One culinary thread runs through them all – the Japanese potato.
Along with rice, the crop is fiercely protected as one of only a few homegrown staples in a country that imports more than 60% of its food.
But that could be about to change. Under pressure from Donald Trump, Japan is moving towards lifting a 76-year-old ban on imported American potatoes.

Japan’s potato farmers say lifting the ban would threaten their livelihoods, and expose consumers to an inferior product. They worry batches of American potatoes could bring harmful insects and pests into Japanese fields.

Tokyo partially lifted the ban in 2006 to permit imports of US potatoes exclusively to make crisps. The vegetables must be transported in sealed containers and then cooked at a high temperature to prevent the spread of pests and diseases.
But a complete lifting of the ban would put fresh American potatoes on restaurant menus and supermarket shelves for the first time since 1950.

“We have repeatedly and unequivocally stated our opposition to imports,” said Toshihide Numasawa, an employee of the Japan Agriculture group in Hokkaido, where about 80% of the country’s potatoes are grown. He said there were various reasons for the objection, including the “risk of pests and diseases entering the country and damage to Hokkaido’s production areas.”

Potatoes were initially collector’s items for intrigued plant enthusiasts when Dutch traders introduced them to Japan in 1598. By the mid-1800s, potatoes were a nutritious alternative to rice – a crop unsuited to Hokkaido’s cooler climate. Now they are the basis for the perennial favourite jaga bata, a baked version slathered in butter, while poteto sarada has practically achieved national-dish status.

Hokkaido’s best-known variety is the Danshaku (Irish Cobbler), a potato high in starch whose fluffy, absorbent flesh makes them perfect for butter and other toppings or to soak up meat juices in a stew.

“We believe consumers have come to recognise which are best suited to particular dishes,” said Numasawa, adding that Hokkaido potato farmers were also being buffeted by homegrown pest outbreaks, global heating and rural depopulation.

The country now grows more than 90 varieties of potato and Japanese consumers ate 3.5m tons of potatoes in 2024, according to the agriculture ministry, among them 1.2m tons of fresh imports used to make crisps.

The tuber’s place at the centre of Japan-US trade negotiations has created an early headache for Japan’s new agriculture minister, Arata Takebe, whose constituency is located in prime potato-growing country in Hokkaido.
The plan to lift the ban “should progress after thorough scientific and technical discussion” Takebe recently told Jiji Press, adding that a decision could take “considerable time”.
“I know the [US] side has strong expectations, but the ban on imports will not be lifted without sufficient discussions or an agreement acceptable to both sides,” he said.

While potatoes imported for crisps are subject to strict quarantine measures, farmers fear batches of imported fresh potatoes could bring in harmful insects and microbes. Japan’s government has identified 21 pests and diseases that could pose a risk of invasion.

The potato cyst nematode and pale potato cyst nematode are causing most concern. Although they are not a threat to human health, they can damage the vegetable’s roots, which stunts their growth, and remain present in soil for more than 15 years.
Earlier this year, congressional lawmakers urged Trump to continue raising the ban with the Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi.
“US potato growers produce the best potatoes in the world,” they wrote in a letter. “Japan represents a massive market with significant export opportunities for American potato growers.”
After raising the issue during his first term in office, Trump has persuaded Japan’s government to begin talks as he faces accusations that his policies have been “disastrous” for rural America.
Supporters of lifting the ban say it would lower prices for Japanese consumers and bring American farmers an additional $150m a year in export earnings.
But farmers in Hokkaido claim that not enough has been done to eliminate the threat from pests and disease.

“Protecting Hokkaido’s agriculture is not just about protecting Hokkaido,” the Hokkaido Agricultural Corporations Association said in a statement. “It also means protecting the production base that will support Japan’s food supply for the future.”

Naohiro Makino, a potato farmer in Hokkaido, said the ban on fresh potatoes should stay. “Once pests get in, you can’t grow potatoes for more than a decade,” he told the Asahi Shimbun newspaper. “For the sake of the farmland our ancestors protected, I am firmly opposed [to lifting the ban].”

articles.title: Brexit work travel rules need urgent improvement, say UK business leaders
articles.summary: CBI says cross-Channel business trips urgently need to be made easier to support investment and trade
body: Business chiefs have called on the UK government and the European Commission to urgently ease Brexit restrictions on business travel for cross-Channel work trips.

A group representing industry bosses said it wants commitments from Andy Burnham and European political leaders that the restrictions will be one of the priorities in 2027 for furthering ties between the two sides, after a summit in Brussels this week.

The Confederation of British Industry (CBI), which represents some of Britain’s largest companies, welcomed the prime minister’s recent calls for a reset with Europe, designed to reverse some of the damage to Britain’s economy caused by Brexit.

But it said Brexit restrictions, which include making employees obtain work permits for travel, are deterring cross-border investors and hampering trade at the very time both sides are trying to build resilience against China.
Related: Andy Burnham to unveil EU trade deals worth billions of pounds

Sean McGuire, the CBI’s director of Europe and international, said discussions should have been a priority in the talks this week, after a UK-EU summit in 2025 held by Keir Starmer also referenced improving business mobility.
“Very little has been achieved. In fact, practically nothing has been achieved. The emphasis was put on youth mobility,” said McGuire.

EU diplomats have said in the past that the UK pushed hard for improving business mobility but was met with resistance from the bloc, where member states see British services – a big export particularly in the financial sector – as a threat.
McGuire said that energy, defence and car industry bosses say they are being hampered by the inability to travel freely in Europe to service or run multinational operations.
He said the issue should be of interest to all sides as they build on multiple existing laws to protect European supply chains.

“Now that we’ve got youth mobility potentially in the Friday deal, we should move seriously to address the kind of business mobility, which would apply to both the goods sector and the services sector,” he said.
Related: Is £750m a week the real cost of rejoining the EU – or the Brexit bus myth all over again?
British citizens travelling to the EU post-Brexit are restricted to 90 days at a time out of a maximum of 180 days a year, limiting companies’ ability to promote employees and travel.
“If you are a CEO of a multinational you can very quickly clock up 90 days,” McGuire said.

Separately, work permits have to be obtained for each country that a worker travels to. That can affect the servicing of equipment, particularly in engineering, where products that cost millions such as lifts, escalators and factory machines come with service and maintenance contracts.
“There is a big difference between irregular migration, which needs to be tackled, and business mobility, which is bringing investment into the UK and vice versa,” he said.
While an agreement is close on youth mobility, Burnham faces the same roadblock when it comes to opportunities for under-30s, who will be offered a three-year visa scheme to work, travel or study.
“It is a trick because the UK is negotiating with Brussels but work permits are a national competency,” said one EU diplomat.

But McGuire said there is a quick fix for business mobility, involving changes to the annex of the EU-UK trade and cooperation agreement, which allows the two sides to expand visa-free business travel across more industries without reworking the main treaty.

The CBI said it is also “disappointed” that no progress has been made on mutual recognition of qualifications allowing British or EU professionals to practise in each other’s territories as they did before Brexit.
Sources said there was a view in Brussels that mutual recognition of qualifications was more beneficial to the UK than to the EU, causing energy around the talks to drain away.

articles.title: New UK-EU youth mobility scheme may not fully launch until 2030
articles.summary: Exclusive: deal expected to be sealed in principle at EU-UK summit on Friday but trickier elements could be postponed for six months
body: The new post-Brexit UK-EU youth mobility scheme may not come fully into force until 2030.
It will be a disappointment to any under-30s in the UK and the EU who hoped to travel, work or study in each other’s territories from next year after the long-awaited new deal.
EU ambassadors will discuss the latest draft joint statement at a meeting on Wednesday in Brussels, with talk of youth mobility going right to the wire.

“We aim to apply this agreement no later than 2028 and endeavour to ensure that opportunities under the scheme will be available to our young people no later than January 2030,” a draft text agreed by negotiators from London and Brussels says.
The two sides aim to come to a “supplementary agreement” on tuition fees for EU citizens in UK universities.

The text on this most contentious subject is not yet agreed with two alternatives mooted in the draft text – either a deal that students pay a reduced international fee or, alternatively, the same fee as UK nationals. The aim is that this would be agreed separately within six months.

This is to allow linkage with the Made in Europe legislation that will not reach its final stages until possibly April next year in a vote in the European parliament. The legislation is designed to give priority to EU supply chains in the car and other industries.
By linking the two issues the UK can get assurances that the final detail of the deal on mobility cannot be signed off unless it has been included in the Made in Europe legislation.
Related: Burnham says Brexit has dramatically diminished Britain’s global standing
EU countries including Germany could accept an unlimited number of young Britons under a youth mobility scheme, according to sources.

Fresh details on how a scheme might work have emerged with EU leaders and the UK expected to settle on a quota of about 100,000 a year being allowed to work, travel or study in each other’s territories.

The UK has insisted on a quota of EU citizens entering the UK under the scheme to guard against mass migration, but some countries have said they will not follow suit on the other side of the Channel and would be open to taking unlimited numbers.

The quota is expected to be worked out on a country-by-country basis with smaller countries such as Malta and Luxembourg seeking a system that will not be based on a per-capita quota per EU member state.
The new agrifood deal would not be agreed until 1 March 2028, the draft statement seen by the Guardian confirms.

In what looks to be a breakthrough for Burnham there may also be a commitment to enter a dialogue to remove barriers to touring artists, particularly bands and theatres companies that perform in multiple EU member states.
The 72-point joint statement also paves the way for further deals on steel between the UK and the EU.
But there is no agreement yet on whether the UK would commit to dynamically aligning with the EU on trade defence measures such as tariffs on Chinese cars.

The details came as Burnham said there is “no rush” to decide on the UK’s longer-term relationship with the EU, as he came under pressure from his own party to press the brakes on the pace of the rethink.
The prime minister said he would “take stock” of the wider relationship after Friday’s summit in Brussels, at which he also hopes to secure agreements on food and farming and emissions trading.

In an interview with Sky News, Burnham admitted he would now not set out the full options for a closer EU relationship until December – but denied he was “stepping back” from his previous commitments to pursue ties.

articles.title: Caribbean nations fear economic impact of shuttering citizenship program after EU threats
articles.summary: St Kitts and Nevis to wind down citizenship-by-investment program after EU warns of end to visa-free access
body: The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned.

On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis.

Mark Brantley, the premier of Nevis, which has autonomous self-governance in some aspects, said he understood that the “country was given very little choice”, but did not “support the winding down of the program”.

The 42-year-old CBI programme, which St Kitts and Nevis pioneered, allows wealthy foreigners to obtain citizenship and ultimately a passport by investing in infrastructure and other development projects. It has brought billions of dollars into the country and in some years accounted for the largest share of government revenue.

In June, the European Commission wrote to the five Caribbean nations that currently operate CBI programmes: St Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and St Lucia. It warned that countries may lose visa-free access to its 29-country Schengen area if they did not phase out CBI.

In Friday’s statement, Drew blamed concerns over the programme on mismanagement by previous administrations, including years of underselling to undercut other countries, a controversial prison project, weak escrow protections and investment sums not being properly paid into the citizenship unit.

He said his government had led major reforms to the Caribbean’s programmes with international partners, including the US treasury, but argued that continuing the programme risked visa-free travel to parts of Europe and access to international banking. That could disrupt services allowing visitors to use overseas cards and families abroad to send money home.
Brantley, however, argued it was unfair for the EU to force St Kitts and Nevis to make a move without offering assistance to navigate the transition to other industries.

“I have not yet seen from the EU any corresponding suggestions of assistance. And we have to realise that these citizenship-by-investment programs, not only in St Kitts and Nevis, but … smaller countries of the Caribbean, have contributed significantly to our gross domestic product and also to ensuring that our people … can get adequate access to water and to education, to healthcare and the like,” he said.
Brantley described the 1 June 2028 deadline the EU gave the country to phase out the lucrative programme as “frankly ludicrous”.
In his statement, Drew said the CBI programme “did a lot of good, but it also created a danger”.
“When one source pays for half or more of everything, you are at its mercy. If it stops, everything stops. That is putting all of your eggs in one basket,” he added.

The prime minister said the government aimed to diversify its economy by strengthening tourism, yachting, and digital and creative industries, among others. He added that the sale of clean, geothermal energy was “at the heart of it” with drilling and exploration already planned.

“I will not pretend that the road is easy. Less CBI money means we must spend wisely and plan carefully. We will. Our plan is to make this change by growing our economy. Raising taxes is not part of that plan,” Drew said.

Antigua and Barbuda has also expressed willingness to end the programme, though it is trying to negotiate a longer transition period. The five Caribbean governments have taken differing positions on the EU demand. According to local media, Grenada has indicated it wants its programme to continue until 2032, while Dominica and St Lucia have responded to Brussels without publicly committing to ending their programmes.
Jermine Abel in Basseterre contributed reporting

articles.title: Palestinian woman shot dead by Israeli settlers near Jericho, witnesses say
articles.summary: Bullet hit 72-year-old Fadha Wadha in head outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, in the West Bank, say residents
body: A 72-year-old Palestinian woman has been shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli settlers in a village near Jericho where settlers have recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.

Fadha Wadha was standing outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta in the occupied West Bank when she was struck in the head by a bullet as Israeli settlers fired towards Palestinian houses, according to testimonies from residents. Several other Palestinians, including her son, were wounded by gunfire.

Abu Younis, a cousin of Wadha’s husband, told the Guardian that the violence had begun when a group of settlers attacked a young boy they accused of entering a courtyard seized from its Palestinian residents.

Dozens of Israeli settlers, some of them armed, moved into eight buildings in al-Duyuk al-Tahta two weeks ago with the backing of the settler organisation Nachala and a regional council representing illegal settlements in the central West Bank.
Related: Revealed: Israel uploaded millions of photos to Amazon’s facial recognition platform to track Palestinians
“A vehicle carrying settlers chased him,” Younis said. “There were about 15 settlers in several vehicles. They began firing indiscriminately, killing the woman.”
Witnesses said Palestinian residents began to throw stones to defend themselves, as more settlers arrived at the scene, shooting at civilians and injuring six men.

Wadha’s son, Arafat Fidhat, was wounded after he rushed to the scene after learning that his mother had been shot. His wife, Naama Fidhat, told Reuters he was in shock when he accidentally collided with a parked car belonging to one of the settlers.
Witnesses said the vehicle was empty at the time, but that settlers responded by opening fire, wounding Arafat in the torso.

Naama Fidhat said her husband was being taken to a hospital in Ramallah when Israeli soldiers stopped the ambulance and arrested him. She said Israeli soldiers also arrested their son, Wadha’s grandson, early the following morning.
“What did we do? We didn’t do anything,” she said. “This is our house, they were the ones who came with weapons … we were unarmed, we were sleeping.”

The Israeli military said a group of Palestinians in ​a car “accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it”. It said the Palestinians exited the vehicle and attacked the Israelis, who opened fire at the Palestinians. “There are Israeli and Palestinian ​casualties in the incident,” the military said.
The arrival of the Israeli settlers in al-Duyuk al-Tahta had raised fears among Palestinian residents who have faced repeated attacks in the area.

The Binyamin regional council, which covers 47 illegal settlements, claimed the properties in the village had been bought from Palestinians, but Jericho’s governor, Hussein Hamayel, disputed the claim, saying the land belonged to the state and could not legally be sold.
Human rights activists said settlers had assaulted and robbed two Israeli activists and shot a Palestinian man in the leg during the takeover earlier this month.
Related: Ed Miliband announces first sanctions on Israeli firms working in West Bank

“Since the settlers moved into the area on 4 November our lives have been turned upside down,” Younis told the Guardian. “We used to live peacefully and safely on our farms, but since the settlers arrived, our lives have become a living hell. I own 53 dunams [5.3 hectares] of farmland with greenhouses, but we are no longer allowed to access them. We have suffered devastating financial losses, and now people are being killed as well.”

There has been a sharp ​rise in attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians in the West Bank, territory Israel captured in the 1967 six-day war. UN bodies and most ​countries deem the settlements illegal, which Israel disputes.

On Tuesday, Suleiman Abu Srour, a photographer for the Palestinian news agency Wafa, was beaten by Israeli soldiers while covering events in al-Duyuk al-Tahta. Wafa said he suffered fractures and bruises, was detained for six hours and had his phone confiscated before being released.

Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion, ethnic cleansing and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.

articles.title: ‘Godmother’ of illegal Israeli West Bank settler project Daniella Weiss among group sanctioned by Australia
articles.summary: Foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, says rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are ‘extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution’
body: Australia has announced another tranche of sanctions on individuals and organisations involved in “illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians” in the West Bank.
In a statement, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said it was the first time Australian sanctions had targeted a construction company involved in the building of settlements.
The sanctions prohibit Australians and Australian businesses from trading with or providing financial or other support to three individuals and four organisations.
Related: Most Israelis think settlements policy should change to avoid more sanctions, poll finds
“We are taking these actions because the rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution,” Wong’s statement said.
“This includes the E1 settlement where demolitions and the displacement of Palestinians have occurred in recent weeks. Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.”

Among those sanctioned is Daniella Weiss and her Israeli settler organisation, the Nachala movement, which the government said has provided support for outposts and settlements that have perpetrated serious human rights abuses.
Weiss is known as the “godmother” of the settler movement and was sanctioned by the UK in May 2025, shortly after she appeared on Louis Theroux’s documentary The Settlers.
She and Nachala have also advocated for the settlement of Israelis in Gaza and the expulsion of Palestinians from the area.

The 80-year-old was previously the mayor of Kedumim, an Israeli settlement in the West Bank where far-right Israeli minister Bezalel Smotrich, who has also been sanctioned by the Australian government, also lives.

Prominent West Bank settler Eliav Libi has also been sanctioned, as well as the Eyal Hari Yehuda construction company which has helped develop settlements and outposts and demolished Palestinian structures in the West Bank.

Wong said the sanctioned individuals and organisations had “actively participated in the planning, coordination and establishment of new settlements, including raising funds, recruitment of volunteers and providing support to violent settlers”.
The government said the sanctions were coordinated with the UK, who announced sanctions on Israeli companies planning to build illegal settlements.
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said the “status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable”.

“That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution. And we will not stand by while those blocking desperately needed aid deepen the intolerable suffering of civilians in Gaza.”
More settlements had been approved under the four years of Benjamin Netanyahu’s government than in the previous 20 years.
Israel’s possible new prime minister, Gadi Eisenkot, has said that he would take a tougher approach than Netanyahu on settler violence.
Wong said she had spoken to her Israeli counterpart, Gideon Sa’ar, on Tuesday night, and outlined Australia’s position.
“We’ve made clear we will continue to take action in respect of those involved in the settlement enterprise. The settlement enterprise is violent.”
Wong had signalled further sanctions in September, after the government ruled out an import ban on trade from illegal settlements in the West Bank.
Recent analysis by human rights organisation Global Echo showed 85 of 132 food shipments over eight years had contained more than US$5m of organic dates grown in settlements.
Related: Food grown in illegal West Bank settlements being sold in Australia as ‘produce of Israel’
On Wednesday, the foreign affairs minister said the government was still considering further action.
“We’ll continue to look at targeted measures we can take to push back against what the current Israeli government is doing,” Wong told journalists.
When asked whether Wong was concerned Israel would respond to Australian sanctions with countermeasures, the minister said it had done in the past.

“We’ve seen the Israeli government take action against Australia, including asking our diplomats to leave Ramallah. We’ve also seen the [now] caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu, be very public in his criticism of Australia.
“So obviously, there is a reaction to Australia acting, but we think this is the right thing to do.”
The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, said the sanctions did not go far enough to stop illegal settlements or take action against the Israeli government.
The minor party has pushed the government to join other nations including the UK and Canada to ban imports of products made in illegal settlements.
“This announcement won’t touch most of the hundreds of businesses that have a role in this brazen breach of international law, or the Israeli government that backs them,” Shoebridge said.
The government warned Australian businesses they must not bid for construction tenders for illegal settlement developments.
Individuals breaching sanctions can attract a penalty of up to 10 years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to $910,000 or three times the value of the relevant transaction.
Businesses can be fined up to $3.64m or three times the value of the relevant transaction.
The Australia Palestine Advocacy Network president, Nasser Mashni, pushed for further sanctions against individuals, companies and the Israeli government.
“Australia has sanctioned a company that builds illegal settlements. Now sanction the Israeli government that orders Palestinian homes demolished,” he said.

articles.title: Joy, hope and anger as Serbia student movement’s political novices enter parliament
articles.summary: Celebrating supporters say they feel vindicated by arrival of Student List candidates in national assembly
body: The paved plateau in front of Serbia’s national assembly became an impromptu dancefloor, as people of all ages joyfully whirled in a kolo. Drivers passing by sounded their horns, while hundreds of people waved flags, blew whistles and cheered. Every now and again, the crowd parted, allowing smartly dressed men and women to walk up the steps and into the building.

These were the candidates from the Student List, on their way to being sworn in as members of parliament after their stunning victory in last month’s parliamentary elections. Those who had come to cheer them on displayed their feelings on badges, flags and placards.
Related: Serbia’s Student List candidates sworn in as MPs after election triumph

“Srećan rad” was a common sentiment – “Good luck with your work”. Another ubiquitous slogan revived the catchphrase of a politically ambitious young girl from a popular 1990s sitcom, Open Doors (Otvorena vrata) – “the assembly is starting”.

Tuesday’s delight echoed the euphoria of election night, when the Student List’s collection of political novices defeated the long-serving populist leader Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS).

A group from the Belgrade suburb of Zemun were among the crowd, including Lijlana, who was holding a sign reading: “What one person cannot do, 3 can” – a reference to the Student List’s number on the ballot papers.

“This is the voice of the people,” she said. “People who want peace, who want the government to do their job, who want to have institutions that are operating in favour of people, not in favour of the mafia.”
Her friend Jelena agreed. “This is an historic moment for Serbia,” she said.

Members of Serbia’s student movement were also on the assembly steps. They said they were feeling vindication that two years of youth-led protests had produced such a stunning result, and hopeful about the Student List’s prospects in government.

“We are celebrating winning against the regime of Aleksandar Vučić,” said Aleksandar, a political science student at Belgrade university. “I want the new government to make a better life for us,” added his classmate Iva.

But in some quarters, anger remains the dominant emotion. The protests were triggered by the deaths of 16 people after a canopy collapsed at a renovated railway station in Serbia’s second city, Novi Sad. The students blamed endemic corruption, and held Vučić and the SNS responsible.

Judging by some of the placards outside the assembly, forgiveness seems unlikely. One sign suggested that erstwhile SNS ministers should “end up like Elena and Nicolae Ceaușescu,” Romania’s former first couple, who were executed after a show trial in 1989.

In fact, most of the SNS members who arrived for the inaugural session faced nothing worse than jeers, with the exception of Lidija Vukićević. A woman in the crowd poured a bottle of drinking yoghurt over her head, prompting Vukićević to criticise the “primitivism and vulgarity” of Student List supporters. The incident also allowed Vučić to push his narrative that the students were promoting a regime of “naked terror” by targeting SNS members for harassment and arrest. All they could offer Serbia was “hatred and yoghurt”, he said.

The student movement was quick to condemn the incident, with one faculty group posting that it was “not in line with the values we stand for and fight for”. It urged supporters “to treat all fellow citizens peacefully and with dignity, regardless of their political affiliation”.

Inside the assembly, it did not take long for the new intake to be sworn in as MPs. Hundreds of journalists and photographers crammed into the debating chamber to witness the ceremony marking the end of 14 years of SNS government. It was a discombobulating experience for some, with Bojan Dimitrijević, who until recently was best known as an actor, needing to be reminded he was now an MP, rather than a candidate.

“In my theatre work we make illusions to illustrate some truths, but here we are making some realistic things that will change the imagination of the people,” said the 53-year-old, who worked with Samantha Morton and John Hurt in the TV series The Last Panthers. He said he was particularly concerned with culture and ecology, but conceded that he did not know “where to start with fixing every problem we have here”.

If nothing else, the Student List can call on expertise from a wide range of professions. Dimitrijević’s fellow MPs include the former basketball player Dejan Bodiroga, a high-school English teacher, Katarina Šćepanović, and Dejan Šoškić, a former governor of the National Bank of Serbia. Keen to get on with forming a government, they found themselves frustrated on their first day in the job by SNS delaying tactics.

Vučić, now in opposition, addressed the assembly for more than 90 minutes, while the acting speaker, Stojan Radenović, called regular extended breaks. The cardiologist Ilija Srdanović, who topped the Student List’s candidate list, said this was pointless and expensive, describing “every day of delay in decision-making” as “a burden on the citizens of Serbia”.
On the sunny plateau outside the building, small groups of Student List supporters seemed unfazed. Some of them had waited 14 years to see Vučić out of office.

Standing alongside her friends from Zemun, Jelena put it in perspective. “This is just the starting day of the democratic era in Serbia,” she said. The SNS can only delay; with a 30-seat working majority, the Student List now holds the power.

articles.title: Anti-Arab hate speech surged on social media during Israel’s election, report finds
articles.summary: Digital monitors recorded 400% rise in posts attacking Arab Israelis, including Netanyahu’s disproven fraud allegations
body: Anti-Arab hate speech surged on social media in Israel around the country’s general election last month, digital monitors have said, as politicians including Benjamin Netanyahu levelled disproven allegations against Arab Israeli parties of election fraud.

A new report by the Israel-based Brandeis Institute and FakeReporter recorded a deluge of anti-Arab discourse across social media platforms such as X, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok in the days surrounding Israel’s 27 October election.
According to FakeReporter’s analysis, anti-Arab sentiment on X rose by more than 400% from election day on 27 October to 29 October. Similar content also spread across Facebook and other platforms.

Arab-majority parties won 19 seats in the Israeli Knesset in last month’s election, potentially putting them in a kingmaker position. The opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been invited to try to put together a coalition to replace Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist government.

The posts mainly pushed three messages, the first of which was the allegation that “the Arabs stole the election” via fraud, vote buying and foreign interference, according to the report. Israel’s electoral commission had already publicly refuted such claims.
Posts also depicted Arab citizens of Israel as a security threat and called for them to have their right to vote restricted.

Some of the most-viewed posts also came from top Israeli officials and Netanyahu’s post “They stole the election in Israel!” was viewed 1.2m times. A post by the far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, calling for heads of Arab political parties was also viewed more than 350,000 times.

FakeReporter said much of the anti-Arab hate speech was fuelled by politicians from Netanyahu’s political bloc. “It can be said that they were a major factor in spreading hate speech against Arab citizens of Israel following the election,” its analysis said.

Arab citizens of Israel, the majority of whom are Palestinians, make up 21% of the population of Israel. Since the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack and Israel’s subsequent war in Gaza, Arab political leaders have faced increasingly inflammatory attacks and accusations of dual loyalties.

In the run-up to the election, Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted to bar the country’s two main Arab majority political lists from running – a move later struck down by the Israeli supreme court.
Eisenkot last week condemned what he called a “racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation” against the country’s Arab citizens.

The Brandeis Institute and FakeReporter sent letters to Google, Meta, TikTok and X on 4 November calling on them to take steps to stop the proliferation of hate speech against Arab citizens of Israel on their platforms.

Only Google responded, saying that Israel’s election is a “Priority 0” for the company and that it has dedicated resources to monitoring traffic around the election, but that the Central Elections Committee had made no requests for extra moderation procedures.
